name: Kleene normal form

name: Rice theorem pattern
statement: Any nontrivial extensional property of one-place partial recursive functions has a nonrecursive index set.
conditions: C is a nontrivial class of one-place partial recursive functions.
The index set contains exactly indices e such that the e-th partial recursive function belongs to C.
Membership depends only on the computed partial function, not on the program text.
conclusion: The index set for C is not recursive.
typical_uses: Show program semantic properties are undecidable.
Repair reductions from halting-style problems.
common_misuses: Applying Rice's theorem to syntactic properties of programs rather than extensional function properties.
Forgetting the nontriviality condition.
bridge_lemmas: There are indices for functions inside and outside the class.
A hypothetical decider can be used to decide a known undecidable set by constructing suitable indices.
repair_templates: Verify the property is extensional and nontrivial, then reduce a standard undecidable index set to it.

name: Full second-order quantification
statement: In full second-order semantics, predicate variables of arity n range over all n-ary relations on the universe, while individual variables range over elements.
conditions: A second-order language is fixed.
Full semantics, not general/Henkin semantics, is intended.
conclusion: Satisfaction clauses for second-order quantifiers quantify over all relations of the appropriate arity.
typical_uses: Check whether compactness or Lowenheim-Skolem may be used.
Repair arguments that confuse full and Henkin second-order semantics.
common_misuses: Applying first-order completeness, compactness, or Lowenheim-Skolem directly to full second-order logic.
Letting predicate variables range only over definable relations without saying so.
bridge_lemmas: For forall X phi, satisfaction requires phi for every relation assigned to X.
General models restrict the range of predicate variables to specified relation collections.
repair_templates: State whether semantics is full or general before using model-theoretic theorems.

name: Second-order induction categoricity of natural numbers
statement: The second-order induction axiom for zero and successor forces every element to lie in the successor-closure of zero, yielding categoricity of the standard natural-number structure under the usual successor axioms.
conditions: The structure has a distinguished zero and successor satisfying the usual zero-not-successor and injective-successor conditions.
The full second-order induction principle holds for all subsets of the universe.
conclusion: The structure is isomorphic to the standard natural-number successor structure.
typical_uses: Explain why full second-order arithmetic can be categorical while first-order arithmetic has nonstandard models.
Repair categoricity arguments by identifying the use of full second-order induction.
common_misuses: Using first-order induction schema as if it quantified over all subsets.
Forgetting that Henkin/general semantics may not give categoricity.
bridge_lemmas: The intersection of all inductive subsets is the standard successor closure.
Full second-order quantification includes that closure as a predicate candidate.
repair_templates: Specify full second-order semantics and the complete induction axiom before concluding categoricity.

name: Failure of compactness for full second-order logic
statement: There is a set of full second-order sentences such that every finite subset is satisfiable but the whole set is not satisfiable.
conditions: Full second-order semantics is used.
conclusion: The compactness theorem fails for full second-order logic.

name: Failure of Lowenheim-Skolem for full second-order logic
statement: Full second-order logic can characterize structures up to isomorphism in a fixed uncountable cardinality, so the downward Lowenheim-Skolem theorem fails for full second-order semantics.
conditions: Full second-order semantics is used.
A categorical second-order characterization such as the real ordered field or standard arithmetic context is available.
conclusion: A satisfiable full second-order theory need not have a countable model.

Explain how second-order categoricity avoids first-order nonstandardness.

Isomorphic structures must have the same cardinality.
repair_templates: Check the semantic regime; if full second-order, do not cite first-order Lowenheim-Skolem.

name: Skolem normal form
statement: Every first-order formula can be transformed, for satisfiability or consequence purposes in the stated setting, into a form whose quantifiers are universal after adding suitable Skolem function symbols for existential dependencies.
conditions: A first-order formula is given.
The language may be expanded by new Skolem function symbols as needed.
The transformation is used with the theorem's equivalence or satisfiability-preservation conditions.
conclusion: There is a corresponding Skolem normal form with only universal quantifiers in front of a quantifier-free matrix.

Expanding a model with Skolem functions preserves satisfiability in the intended direction.

name: Translation between many-sorted and one-sorted logic
statement: Many-sorted first-order logic can be translated into ordinary one-sorted first-order logic using unary predicates for sorts and relativized quantifiers, preserving truth under the associated structures.
conditions: A many-sorted language and structure are given.
Sort predicates or domains are represented in the one-sorted translation.
Functions and relations respect their declared sorts.
conclusion: A many-sorted sentence is true in the many-sorted structure iff its translation is true in the associated one-sorted structure.

name: Compactness for many-sorted first-order logic
statement: A set of many-sorted first-order sentences has a model if every finite subset has a model, using the translation to ordinary first-order logic.

name: General models for second-order logic
statement: A general second-order model consists of a first-order universe together with specified collections of relations that serve as the ranges of predicate variables, rather than all possible relations.
